 Tulsa County shares early voting success, winter preparation
 Commissioner Lonnie Sims discusses increased early voting, a new five-year jail agreement with Tulsa and the county’s preparations for winter weather.
 Erin Conrad 
 November 17, 2026 05:14 PM 1 min read 
 Copy 
 Link copied 
 Email
 Print
 Tulsa Co Commissioner Lonnie Sims talks early voting success, new jail agreement, and if the county is ready for the winter
 TULSA COUNTY, Okla. - Tulsa County Commissioner Lonnie Sims says several county efforts are showing results, from expanded early voting locations to a new agreement with the City of Tulsa on jail operations.
 Sims also outlined how the county is preparing for winter weather, including supplies, road treatments and around-the-clock operations during a storm.
 Early voting expands across Tulsa County
 Sims credited Gwen Freeman and her team with researching and developing a plan that increased early voting this year.
 He said Tulsa County had about 10,000 more early voters than it did in 2022, nearly doubling the number of people who voted early.
 The county offered four early voting locations, including a first-time location on the west side at Chandler Park.
 New jail agreement aims to save taxpayer money
 Tulsa County and the City of Tulsa reached a five-year agreement for jail services after the city closed its municipal jail in July and the two governments began operating under an interim agreement.
 Sims said Sheriff Vic Regalado, Tulsa’s mayor and the mayor’s team led the negotiations. He described the agreement as an opportunity for both governments to collaborate and use resources more efficiently.
 The agreement allows the county to bring in inmates facing municipal and state charges. Sims said the arrangement could create significant cost savings for both Tulsa County and the city.
 The next step is working through operational details, including booking procedures and the day-to-day process for handling inmates.
 County prepares equipment and supplies for winter weather
 Sims said the county’s approach to winter weather is to prepare for changing conditions and have resources ready before a storm arrives.
 Tulsa County has nearly 8,000 tons of sand and salt available, along with about 16,000 gallons of brine to pretreat roads.
 Crews focus on bridges, hillsides and other areas considered higher risk for drivers.
 During a winter storm, county operations shift to a 24-hour schedule. Sims said crews work to keep roads passable, particularly for emergency responders who need to reach people during severe weather.
